{"id": "2:40/q18", "question": "What covenant must Israel fulfill?", "turns_on": "Unspecified covenant: all obligations or a specific historical or inward pledge.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q18/p1", "position": "All commands, prohibitions, faith and obedience, including Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and the majority give the broad view. Ibn Ashur cites 5:12-13, 5:70-71, 2:84-85 and Jewish scriptures: worship, prayer, alms, support for messengers, no bloodshed and fidelity to all revelation."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p2", "position": "Believe and follow Muhammad as foretold, disclosing his description.", "reasons": "Tabari cites 5:12 and 7:157; Kalbi reports the unlettered prophet of Ishmael's line with double reward; Zajjaj cites 3:187; Kashshaf points to 2:41. Razi debates explicitness and concealment."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p3", "position": "Keep the specific 5:12 pledge with twelve chiefs.", "reasons": "It requires prayer, alms, belief in messengers and a good loan; it promises forgiveness and gardens. Muqatil, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj identify it."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p4", "position": "Hold fast to Torah under the Sinai pledge.", "reasons": "Hasan links it to the raised mountain and 2:63; others cite 2:93."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p5", "position": "Worship God alone and follow Islam.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya calls the covenant Islam; Muqatil and Thalabi cite 2:83."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p6", "position": "Thank God for disclosed favors.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Razi report that disclosure binds them to gratitude; Study Quran generalizes it."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p7", "position": "Do not flee battle.", "reasons": "Ismail ibn Ziyad cites 8:15-16 and 33:15; Abu Hayyan adds Paradise as reward."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p8", "position": "Keep the primordial pledge of assent and service.", "reasons": "Sulami's Baghdadis and Bursevi recall pretemporal assent; Qushayri pairs acceptance with fulfillment at return."}, {"id": "2:40/q18/p9", "position": "Guard trusts, secrets, manners, self, reliance and sincerity inwardly.", "reasons": "Sulami gives distinct reciprocal pairs: trusts/treasuries, duties/acceptance, struggle/help, manners/adornment, reliance/sufficiency, worship/stations, service/vision. Qushayri and Abu Hayyan add knowledge, love, contentment and proximity; Qurtubi reports such readings."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q19", "question": "What does God promise in return?", "turns_on": "The promised outcome varies with the proposed human commitment.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q19/p1", "position": "Acceptance, forgiveness, reward and Paradise.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari cite 5:12; Ibn Abbas adds divine pleasure; Qurtubi says obedience signals rather than causes gracious reward; a Prophetic report promises Paradise."}, {"id": "2:40/q19/p2", "position": "Lift burdens and fetters when Israel follows Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says prior burdens followed sins; Tabari, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and Elmali link release to prophetic belief."}, {"id": "2:40/q19/p3", "position": "Give double reward to People of Scripture who follow earlier prophets and Muhammad.", "reasons": "Kalbi transmits forgiveness, Paradise and two rewards; Razi cites 28:52-54, 57:28 and a hadith on three double-reward groups."}, {"id": "2:40/q19/p4", "position": "Give worldly security, sufficiency and victory.", "reasons": "Biqai cites Torah language of livelihood and freedom from fear; Elmali relates 2:38; Sulami and Qushayri pair reliance with sufficiency."}, {"id": "2:40/q19/p5", "position": "Give inward help, nearness, vision and communion.", "reasons": "Sulami, Qushayri, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi describe levels from confession and protection to unity and encounter."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q20", "question": "How are the two covenants annexed?", "turns_on": "Whether annexation names maker or beneficiary, and whether the promise is causal.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q20/p1", "position": "Either party may be named as maker or beneficiary.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Samin discuss subject/object annexation; Baydawi and Alusi prefer God's initiating command and promised reward; Alusi notes a caveat to both as object genitives."}, {"id": "2:40/q20/p2", "position": "Reciprocal language expresses command and promised reward.", "reasons": "Razi says God cannot be commanded, so divine 'covenant' differs from human obligation, as in reciprocal plotting/deceiving language."}, {"id": "2:40/q20/p3", "position": "Human fulfillment signals, rather than causes, God's gracious act.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi reject a causal obligation upon God."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q21", "question": "What do awfū and awfi mean?", "turns_on": "Whether doubling intensifies or simply varies the form.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q21/p1", "position": "Awfā, wafā and waffā can all mean fulfilling a covenant.", "reasons": "Zajjaj prefers Qur'anic awfā; Ibn Awf's verse combines forms; Farra distinguishes Hijaz and Najd; Ibn Qutayba allows both for covenants but only awfā for fully measuring; Abu al-Haytham rejects Shammar's distinction."}, {"id": "2:40/q21/p2", "position": "Awfā can also mean rise or ascend.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite a poem; Shammar distinguishes rights fully paid from mere completion."}, {"id": "2:40/q21/p3", "position": "A doubled verb can intensify repeated or abundant fulfillment.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni says doubled form is emphatic, comparing 6:160, while his light-form discussion of yudhabbihun says a generic verbal noun may itself indicate repeated action; he cites Arabic poets and morphological variation."}, {"id": "2:40/q21/p4", "position": "The doubled form can be simply synonymous.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Tha'labi permit that account."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q22", "question": "Which doubled fulfillment reading is transmitted?", "turns_on": "Transmission and morphological force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q22/p1", "position": "Al-Zuhrī reads doubled fāʾ, sometimes in both clauses.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Ibn Jinni and later writers report it, differing on the first clause and vowel detail; Baydawi reports a doubled wāw."}, {"id": "2:40/q22/p2", "position": "The common light form remains the basis of comparison.", "reasons": "The doubled form can imply amplification rather than a new obligation."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q23", "question": "Why is awfi jussive?", "turns_on": "Whether the command or an elided condition governs.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q23/p1", "position": "The imperative itself carries conditional force and licenses the response.", "reasons": "Nahhas and al-Khalil describe it; Abu al-Hasan ibn Khuruf and one Sibawayh account support direct licensing."}, {"id": "2:40/q23/p2", "position": "An elided if-clause governs the jussive.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi and al-Sirafi supply 'if you fulfill'; Abu Hayyan reports Sibawayh citing al-Khalil for this account."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q24", "question": "What does rahbah mean?", "turns_on": "Whether caution is intrinsic to rahbah.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q24/p1", "position": "Fear, dread or apprehension, often with caution.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites the fear/mercy proverb; Tabrisi contrasts desire; Abu Hayyan records vocalizations and a breastbone derivation; Baydawi and Alusi distinguish wary fear from taqwa."}, {"id": "2:40/q24/p2", "position": "Fear rests on belief about harm and benefit.", "reasons": "Jishumi says perceived harm prompts avoidance and perceived benefit prompts action."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q25", "question": "What are they to fear?", "turns_on": "The feared consequence and scope of the immediate covenant.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q25/p1", "position": "God alone, especially when breaking covenant or denying Muhammad.", "reasons": "Muqatil warns of Hell for denial; Tabari warns of punishment unless they repent; Wahidi, Baghawi and Tabrisi focus on breach; Baydawi and Alusi extend fear to all deeds."}, {"id": "2:40/q25/p2", "position": "Ancestral calamities, including transformation.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas' warning recurs in Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Alusi."}, {"id": "2:40/q25/p3", "position": "Future punishment under certain or uncertain accountability.", "reasons": "Razi says prophets and angels may fear the future (16:50); uncertainty about past obedience creates further fear."}, {"id": "2:40/q25/p4", "position": "Fear rabbis no more; follow the promised messenger.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says leaders obstructed covenant keeping; Elmali distinguishes common people and elites in 2:40-41."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q26", "question": "What force does fronting Me add?", "turns_on": "Whether fronting alone suffices or the combined construction does.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q26/p1", "position": "It intensifies exclusive fear of God.", "reasons": "Kashshaf compares 1:5; Baydawi cites fronting and repeated object; Alusi adds fa and implied condition; Ibn Ashur details four ascending emphases and cites feared leaders; Qushayri invokes God's sole creative power."}, {"id": "2:40/q26/p2", "position": "Fronting alone does not always restrict.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan rejects Zamakhshari's stated basis; Ibn Ashur rejects Sakkaki's placement account and cites Zuhayr for a nonexclusive example."}, {"id": "2:40/q26/p3", "position": "The exclusivity extends to hope and divine decree.", "reasons": "Razi argues independent human action would require fearing others and oneself."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q27", "question": "What governs iyyāya?", "turns_on": "Whether the governor is elided, spoken after rearrangement, or nominal.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q27/p1", "position": "An elided imperative governs the detached accusative.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Jishumi and others say the overt verb already has its attached object; Samin prefers a postposed estimate; Burhan places this in the general elided-governor category and compares other constructions."}, {"id": "2:40/q27/p2", "position": "The construction may be nominal or governed by the overt verb aft

{"id": "2:40/q28", "question": "What does fa do in fa-rhabūn?", "turns_on": "Whether fa is conditional, coordinate or pleonastic.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q28/p1", "position": "It marks an implied condition: if anything is feared, fear Me.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Bursevi make it explicit; Ibn Ashur calls it universal and cites 74:3; Abu Hayyan discusses an elided attention command."}, {"id": "2:40/q28/p2", "position": "It coordinates an elided command with the overt command.", "reasons": "Al-Miftah proposes continued or heightened fear; Alusi objects to simple coordination of two particles but admits a refined elliptical account; later scholars prefer it."}, {"id": "2:40/q28/p3", "position": "It is extra.", "reasons": "Samin reports this analysis."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q29", "question": "How is the final yāʾ read?", "turns_on": "Codex spelling, pause practice, dialect and transmission.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q29/p1", "position": "Most omit it at verse end, even in connection.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi cite cadence; Jishumi cites codex and ease; Ibn Ashur invokes Hudhayl dialect, pause treatment and Sibawayh; Tabrisi notes nūn kasra."}, {"id": "2:40/q29/p2", "position": "Yaʿqūb and some others retain it.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Ibn Atiyya name Ibn Abi Ishaq; Tabrisi names Ibn Kathir in connection; Nashr and Ibn Ashur report Ya'qub in pause and connection, matching Hijazi usage."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q30", "question": "What inward meanings are given to fear?", "turns_on": "Punishment, thoughts or divine majesty as the object.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q30/p1", "position": "Fear is inner light and certainty reached by striving.", "reasons": "Tustari joins piety, tawhid, heart sight and trust; nearness excludes indwelling or union; certainty affects the Resurrection scale."}, {"id": "2:40/q30/p2", "position": "Awe guards the heart's thoughts and belongs to knowledge.", "reasons": "Sulami defines inner apprehension; Sahl contrasts awe in certainty with piety under divine stratagem."}, {"id": "2:40/q30/p3", "position": "Punishment fear is temporary; awe of majesty endures.", "reasons": "Razi's gnostics, Abu Hayyan and Alusi distinguish outward practitioners and people of the heart."}, {"id": "2:40/q30/p4", "position": "Fear now brings security on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Razi reports the saying that God does not combine two fears or securities; greater present fear yields greater future safety."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q31", "question": "What obligations and theological principles does the verse establish?", "turns_on": "The basis of reciprocal promise and human duty.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q31/p1", "position": "Gratitude, covenant fidelity and fear are duties.", "reasons": "Tabrisi calls concealing favor a grave sin; Razi says favor and prior pledge aggravate breach; Baydawi and Bursevi summarize promise and threat."}, {"id": "2:40/q31/p2", "position": "Human acts are real.", "reasons": "Tabrisi argues denial would void covenant, command, promise, threat, messenger and scripture."}, {"id": "2:40/q31/p3", "position": "God's promised reward must occur because His report is truthful.", "reasons": "Razi rejects Mu'tazili rational indebtedness and his Ash'ari school's bare denial as complete accounts, preferring truthful promise."}, {"id": "2:40/q31/p4", "position": "Only God deserves praise and fear as creator.", "reasons": "Razi says idols cannot benefit or harm (26:72-73 etc); Qushayri says a powerless being is not feared."}, {"id": "2:40/q31/p5", "position": "Muhammad's mission addresses Israelites too.", "reasons": "Razi draws this from the passage; Ibn Kathir calls them to Islam."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q32", "question": "How does the address fit the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "How the universal call gives way to ancestral history.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q32/p1", "position": "It turns from general proofs and Adam to Israel's favors and duties.", "reasons": "Tabari says Jewish knowledge of ancestral reports confirms revelation; Razi charts invitation, inducement, warning and detailed favors; Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Kur'an Yolu explain the turn to the People of Scripture. Tabatabai counts twelve episodes of rescue, Sinai, calf, thunderbolt and revival, showing care despite ingratitude. The cited Ma'tarak al-Aqran contrasts Baqarah's reminder of blessings to the Children of Israel with A'raf's reproach for seeking an idol and later worshipping the calf; it says each narrative frame shapes the wording (2:40, 2:58; 7:138, 7:148, 7:161)."}, {"id": "2:40/q32/p2", "position": "Israel is led from favor to Benefactor; Muhammad's community from Benefactor to favor.", "reasons": "Sulami, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi compare 2:152."}, {"id": "2:40/q32/p3", "position": "It pairs encouragement with warning and closes in submission.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan describe the sequence of promise, faith, bodily/financial duties and final fear."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q33", "question": "What earlier-scripture evidence points to Muhammad?", "turns_on": "How explicit and identifiable the predictions were.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q33/p1", "position": "Prior scriptures are read as promising Muhammad.", "reasons": "Razi adduces Deuteronomy's prophet from Israel's brothers, Paran, Habakkuk, Isaiah's city, Ishmael's great nation, Abraham's prayer, Jesus' Ahmad and Paraclete announcements, and Daniel's stone kingdom. He replies to objections about 'among you,' Paran as fire, Jerusalem and the Messiah; Ibn Razin and Christian transmissions give variants."}, {"id": "2:40/q33/p2", "position": "The predictions may have been obscure or known only to a few.", "reasons": "Razi says explicit public time and place would be hard to hide, prompting some to favor a general covenant; defenders say the details were not universally plain."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q34", "question": "How does covenant language illuminate 'I seek refuge in God'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q34/p1", "position": "Seeking refuge is a prayer for protection under reciprocal servitude and lordship.", "reasons": "Razi says the declarative form asks protection, and discusses the present/future imperfect, first-person self-narration and bāʾ attachment."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q35", "question": "What wider conduct is drawn from the command passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q35/p1", "position": "Keeping commands requires abstaining from hidden and public wrongs and excess.", "reasons": "Biqai transmits Harali on greed, usury, spying, mockery, sexual misconduct and pride; worship without abstinence is medicine without diet. The Qur'an can guide or testify against; lawful breadth permits gratitude and restrictions cultivate patience."}, {"id": "2:40/q35/p2", "position": "An unattributed dialogue depicts temptations opposed to obedience.", "reasons": "Durr lists corrupt book, recitation, food, drink, house, snares, caller and market."}]}
{"id": "2:40/q36", "question": "What does divine speech allow commentators to say?", "turns_on": "Whether the common idiom is permissible.", "positions": [{"id": "2:40/q36/p1", "position": "Arabic idiom permits 'God narrated' when a verse or expression is the subject.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites primordial covenant wording, Abu Amir's verse, Umm Salama, 'God knows' and al-Ajjaj; he avoids the idiom when possible but defends it. Abu Ali questions one poetic proof as possibly erroneous."}, {"id": "2:40/q36/p2", "position": "Some legal theorists prohibit such divine attributions.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports and answers the objection."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q01", "question": "What does the opening question do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q01/p1", "position": "It affirms their conduct while rebuking it, often with astonishment and threat.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī call the hamza interrogative in form and a statement of their actual course; al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, and al-Itqān add astonishment. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān stress censure. Al-Samīn also gives denial or wonder."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q02", "question": "What does the verb 'command' mean and how is it constructed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q02/p1", "position": "It directs someone to act and governs a person and a commanded act.", "reasons": "Jishumī defines a command as a superior's utterance to a subordinate, literal of speech and figurative of action. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn describe two complements, al-nās direct and bi-l-birr prepositional; poetry licenses occasional omission of the preposition. Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes amr 'affair' and notes imperative hamza loss or retention after conjunction."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q03", "question": "Who are the 'people' being commanded?", "turns_on": "Whether the address concerns scholars or Israelites broadly and whether the audience is their followers, Arabs, or anyone besides them.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q03/p1", "position": "Muslim kin and others privately advised.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Tustarī, Ibn ʿAbbās accounts and later commentators mention companions, in-laws, milk kin, relatives and allies; this overlap is recorded in the occasion question."}, {"id": "2:44/q03/p2", "position": "Ordinary Jewish followers or common people.", "reasons": "Bursevī identifies lower-status common folk; Ibn ʿĀshūr says this follows if the address is specifically to scholars."}, {"id": "2:44/q03/p3", "position": "Arab questioners or polytheists.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentions Arab questioners; Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes Jewish descriptions of their religion and 2:89 if the addressees are all Isr

{"id": "2:44/q04", "question": "What does birr mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q04/p1", "position": "Expansive goodness, kindness, obedience, piety, or any virtuous deed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites reports of obedience; al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı relate breadth to open land and say it embraces all good. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and Study Quran include truthfulness, obedience, kinship, or piety. Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī discuss kindness and the hirr/birr proverb; al-Akhfash takes it as hissing versus kindness, al-Māzinī as cat versus mouse. Ibn al-Jawzī gives benefit to the recipient and Qur'anic senses of kinship (2:224, 60:8), obedience (5:2, 19:14, 19:32, 58:9, 83:18), and piety (2:177). Al-Ṭabrisī says birr requires intention unlike accidental khayr. Al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn give rare senses heart, fox cub, sheep-driving, and lexical poetry. Al-Rāzī cites 2:189; al-Bayḍāwī and Elmalılı classify devotion to God, kin, and others. Study Quran cites 2:177, 2:189, 3:92 and rewards of abrār at 3:193, 76:5, 82:13."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q05", "question": "Which good act is meant by birr in this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports specify different acts under the word's broad sense; some commentators say the cases converge or more than one occasion is possible.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q05/p1", "position": "Belief in and following Muhammad, including keeping the covenant recorded in the Torah.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Jews recognized his truth; Ibn ʿAbbās says they told others not to disbelieve the Torah's prophecy yet broke its covenant, or urged entry into Muhammad's religion. Some foretold him to Arabs before his advent, then rejected him. Al-Rāzī and Elmalılı mention fear of losing gifts, payments, taxes or rank. Bursevī distinguishes advice to poor people from delay urged on wealthy people. Al-Biqāʿī calls this the Torah's foundational righteousness. Sources identify Muslim kin, companions or followers as recipients."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p2", "position": "General obedience, piety, good works and avoidance of disobedience.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Suddī give this broad account; al-Ṭabarī says the reports agree on what pleases God while the speakers do otherwise. Ibn Jurayj mentions People of Scripture and hypocrites; al-Qurṭubī considers the explanations close."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p3", "position": "Charity or almsgiving, which they withheld or even diverted.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj relates stinginess to hard hearts, usury and illicit gain. Al-Kashshāf, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī mention embezzled donations; al-Qurṭubī calls this close to other explanations."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p4", "position": "Adherence to the Torah, which they themselves violated by denying its description of Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj calls this primary; Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Isḥāq, al-Baghawī and others say that denying the Prophet, changing the Torah or concealing his description violates the very scripture they commend."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p5", "position": "Specific duties such as prayer, fasting and zakat, which the speakers neglected.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj and Ibn ʿAbbās name fasting, prayer and other commands; Abū Ḥayyān also reports prayer and zakat, while Study Quran includes prayer and alms under piety."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p6", "position": "Inward states or spiritual advance demanded of others while teachers lack corresponding practice.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī and al-Qushayrī contrast demands for inner realities, haste toward God and scrupulous attention to others with outward neglect and one's own heaps of faults; an anonymous poem contrasts a mote and a log. Al-Qushayrī's camels image asks why they water others but do not drink."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p7", "position": "Just dealing in questions without a bribe or personal stake.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says the Jews advised a questioner fairly when no right, bribe or benefit was at issue; Ibn Kathīr transmits the same point."}, {"id": "2:44/q05/p8", "position": "Truthfulness, which they urged without practicing.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this variant along with other readings to Qatāda, Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddī."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q06", "question": "Who is directly rebuked?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is restricted to scholars, covers all Israelites, or shifts to believers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q06/p1", "position": "Jewish scholars or rabbis, especially those in Medina.", "reasons": "Jishumī says scholars agree on the Jewish setting. Many reports identify scholars who instructed Muslim kin or ordinary followers; al-Qurṭubī says commentators direct the interrogative to them. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a collective address whose actual rebuke falls on this subgroup."}, {"id": "2:44/q06/p2", "position": "The Children of Israel or People of the Book collectively.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Ṭabarī say Israelites; Ibn Kathīr and al-Durr say People of Scripture. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the direct grammar covers all Israelites, either each as a preacher or by collective attribution."}, {"id": "2:44/q06/p3", "position": "Believers who recite the Qur'an, by a shift in address.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this alongside the Qur'an identification; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī find the shift unlikely, citing the sustained address to the People of the Book; they compare 12:29."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q07", "question": "What does 'you forget' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it is a literal lapse or a deliberate neglect, given the rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q07/p1", "position": "You leave, neglect, or abandon yourselves and your duty.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Samīn and others invoke 9:67; al-Qurṭubī also cites 6:44 and 2:237. Al-Rāzī argues involuntary lapse would not be blameworthy. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī take the wording as 'as though forgotten.' Abū Ḥayyān says this choice intensifies heedlessness; Bursevī distinguishes lapse after knowledge from general inattention. Al-Qurṭubī notes the verbal noun nisyān, rejecting nisayān; and a report says Adam forgot and descendants therefore forget."}, {"id": "2:44/q07/p2", "position": "Literal forgetting is loss of what was once present, a God-created lapse.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī give the cognitive definition; al-Ṭabrisī says sahw may concern something never known. {"id": "2:44/q19", "question": "What does ʿaql mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q19/p1", "position": "Understanding, perception or knowledge that restrains error and wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites the camel hobble, blood money, gazelle, ibex, fortress and stomach medicine; al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī explain restraint. {"id": "2:44/q20", "question": "What is the nature of human reason?", "turns_on": "Whether reason is knowledge, an innate capacity, a light, a substance, or a created accident.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q20/p1", "position": "Reason is knowledge or necessary cognitions that enable moral responsibility and judgment.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives necessary cognitions or knowledge of obligations and good and bad; al-Ṭabrisī and ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā define knowledge restraining evil, adding that stronger restraint means stronger intellect. Al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes completeness of intellect and knowledge and denies predicating intellect of God because He acquires no knowledge and needs no restraint."}, {"id": "2:44/q20/p2", "position": "Reason is a capacity, disposition, discriminating faculty, or means of acquiring insight.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports a capacity to infer unseen from witnessed; al-Ṭabrisī reports discernment or human distinctiveness as close definitions. Al-Ustādh Abū Bakr doubts the 'instrument' attribution, calls it metaphorical for an accident, and describes a means of gaining light and insight rather than a light or form."}, {"id": "2:44/q20/p3", "position": "Reason is a spiritual light by which the soul apprehends knowledge.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Ālūsī describe necessary and theoretical apprehension and restraint; al-Muḥāsibī calls it lights and insights. Al-Ustādh Abū Bakr rejects identifying reason itself as a light."}, {"id": "2:44/q20/p4", "position": "Reason is an eternal subtle or simple substance.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports philosophers' view of an eternal substance, sometimes in the body emitting a discriminating ray. {"id": "2:44/q21", "question": "Where is reason located?", "turns_on": "Whether sensation points to the brain or life and the senses point to the heart.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q21/p1", "position": "In the brain.", "reasons": "A philosophical group and Bursevī give the seat of sensation as their reason."}, {"id": "2:44/q21/p2", "position": "In the heart.", "reasons": "A philosophical group and Bursevī's reported alternative point to the heart as source of life and the senses."}]}
{"id": "2:44/q22", "question": "Does reason vary in people, and do its judgments vary?", "turns_on": "Whether reason itself varies, while rational judgments remain stable.", "positions": [{"id": "2:44/q22/p1", "position": "Reason itself does not vary among people.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this view; al-Ṭabrisī says disputes over its essence do not affect judgments such as a hundred exceeding one or a whole exceeding its part."}, {"id": "2:44/q22/p2", "position": "Reason itself varies, but its judgments do not.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this counterpart; al-Ṭabrisī allows greater restraint to mark greater intelligence through ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā, while maintaining stable rational judgments."}]}
